summary: A 1975 note with observations on the IMP and host protocol changes, drawing on international standards recommendations from IFIP working group 6.1. See also RFC 692, RFC 690 and RFC 687.

plainLanguage.summary: People compared the proposed network changes to what international groups were recommending, and wrote down how they matched.

questions: imp host protocol changes international standards
what did ifip wg 6.1 propose for a packet header
how big was the proposed datagram header
why was 184 bits a problem for the imp host protocol
subtitle: Vinton Cerf compares ARPANET host-IMP protocol changes with a proposed international packet header.

tldr.problem: ARPANET's IMP/Host protocol was being changed while an international working group was recommending a standard packet header for connecting hosts to packet networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the proposed header: a 144-bit layout of small fields and two 48-bit addresses. It then discusses how to fit it with the existing 40-bit Host-to-Host header.
tldr.outcome: The combined 184 bits are called not very pleasant. Several workarounds are offered, each needing changes to existing NCP programs.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 696's status as Unknown and shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a set of comments on proposals, not a specification.

sections.title: Context: An International Header Proposal
sections.content:
Vinton Cerf writes in reference to RFCs 687, 690 and 692 on IMP/Host and Host/IMP protocol changes. He offers observations about a recommendation from working group 6.1 of the International Federation of Information Processing. At a May meeting at the NCC, the group voted to present CCITT with a recommendation for a standard packet (or datagram) header.

The header is meant to interface hosts to packet networks. It is not a Host-to-Host header and not an IMP-to-IMP header. Most of it is address space (96 bits), chosen to be compatible with the current maximum address space of the telephone system (14 digits).
sections.plainLanguage: An international group wanted every packet network to use the same kind of address label. This note says what the label would look like and how ARPANET might fit.

sections.title: The Proposed Header Fields
sections.content:
The fields are: Local Network (4 bits, usable by a local network in any way it wants), Datagram Format (4 bits, which ARPANET could set to binary 1001 to stay compatible with the existing message leader), Packet Type Code (8 bits, usable for the HOST/IMP and IMP/HOST code) and Facilities (16 bits, not yet allocated; possibly for tracing, accounting and class of service, with perhaps 8 bits left to the originating or destination network).

Then Text Length (16 bits) counts the octets of text, excluding the fixed-length header. The 48-bit Destination Address could be split into network identifier (8 bits), host identifier (8 bits), IMP identifier (16 bits) and 16 reserved bits. The 48-bit Source Address would work similarly.
sections.plainLanguage: The label has boxes for where the packet is going, where it came from, how long it is, and some extras. Each box has a set size.

sections.title: Fitting It With the Host-to-Host Header
sections.content:
The resulting packet header is 144 bits long. Adding the present 40-bit Host-to-Host header gives 184 bits, which Cerf calls not very pleasant. A temporary fix, until a new NCP design, would squeeze out the reserved 16-bit fields in the two addresses, giving 32 bits to carry the byte size and byte count.

Other options are to use the length field and a facilities flag to indicate byte size and count, or to add a dummy byte after the 144th bit, followed by the 40 bits of NCP header. That totals 192 bits, a number divisible by 12, 16, 24, 32 and 48. The first two ideas need substantial changes to existing NCP programs and are probably not very palatable.
sections.plainLanguage: The new label plus the old label do not add up to a nice round size. The note suggests a few ways to trim or pad until the pieces fit.

sections.title: Bit Lengths for Text
sections.content: On the proposed text length field, Cerf notes that bit lengths are the most flexible. He says it seems reasonable to admit that nearly all data transmission is done in 8-bit quantities, which would make bit lengths an unnecessary luxury. He adds that this is a weak argument when 36-bit and 32-bit machines must interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Most computers count in groups of eight bits, but some use other sizes, so counting in single bits is still the safest choice.

fields.name: Local Network
fields.desc: Free for the local network to use.

fields.name: Packet Type Code
fields.desc: Could carry the HOST/IMP and IMP/HOST code.

fields.name: Text Length
fields.desc: Octets of text, not counting the header.

fields.name: Destination Address
fields.desc: Network, host and IMP identifiers plus reserved bits.
